```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, out.width = "90%", fig.align = "center")

# Locate the project root (folder containing run_project.R) so paths work no
# matter where the report is rendered from.
find_root <- function(start = getwd()) {
  d <- normalizePath(start, winslash = "/")
  repeat {
    if (file.exists(file.path(d, "run_project.R"))) return(d)
    p <- dirname(d)
    if (identical(p, d)) stop("Project root not found. Render this report from inside the project folder.")
    d <- p
  }
}
root <- find_root()
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = root)

need <- function(rel) {
  p <- file.path(root, rel)
  if (!file.exists(p)) stop("Missing '", rel, "'. Run `Rscript run_project.R` first to generate the analysis results.")
  p
}

info    <- read.csv(need("outputs/tables/dataset_info.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
quality <- read.csv(need("outputs/tables/data_quality_summary.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
outl    <- read.csv(need("outputs/tables/outlier_summary.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
stats_t <- read.csv(need("outputs/tables/summary_statistics.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
gender  <- read.csv(need("outputs/tables/gender_summary.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
corr    <- read.csv(need("outputs/tables/correlation_matrix.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
eval_k  <- read.csv(need("outputs/tables/cluster_evaluation.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
model   <- read.csv(need("outputs/tables/model_evaluation.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
prof    <- read.csv(need("outputs/tables/segment_profiles.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
recs    <- read.csv(need("outputs/tables/business_recommendations.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
seg     <- read.csv(need("data/processed/segmented_customers.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

is_synthetic <- identical(info$Dataset_Type[1], "synthetic")
k_final      <- model$Value[model$Metric == "K (clusters)"]
avg_sil      <- model$Value[model$Metric == "Average silhouette width"]
bss_tss      <- model$Value[model$Metric == "Between-SS / Total-SS (%)"]
n_customers  <- nrow(seg)
largest      <- prof[which.max(prof$Customers), ]
top_spender  <- prof[which.max(prof$Avg_Spending_Score), ]

plot_path <- function(name) file.path("outputs", "plots", name)
```

# Executive Summary

This project segments **`r n_customers` customers** into **`r k_final` groups** using k-means clustering on three standardised variables: age, annual income and spending score. The segmentation has an average silhouette width of **`r avg_sil`**, so cluster separation is `r if (avg_sil >= 0.5) "reasonably strong" else if (avg_sil >= 0.25) "moderate (clusters overlap somewhat)" else "weak"`.

The largest segment is **`r largest$Segment`** (`r largest$Customers` customers, `r largest$Percent`% of the base). The segment with the highest average spending score is **`r top_spender$Segment`** (`r top_spender$Avg_Spending_Score`). Section 9 describes every segment and Section 11 translates them into marketing hypotheses to test. These recommendations are hypotheses, not proven causal effects, and the project does not predict churn.

# Business Problem

Marketing budgets are limited, and treating every customer the same wastes them. A retailer needs to know:

- which customers are the most valuable and deserve loyalty benefits,
- which customers have spending capacity but do not use it,
- which customers spend little and may need a different approach, and
- how to target campaigns instead of sending the same message to everyone.

Customer segmentation answers these questions by grouping customers with similar behaviour.

# Project Objectives

1. Build a reproducible, end-to-end segmentation workflow in R.
2. Clean and validate the data without silently discarding valid observations.
3. Explore age, income, gender and spending patterns.
4. Choose the number of segments using the elbow method and silhouette analysis, with interpretation rather than a single metric.
5. Profile every segment and label it from its observed statistics.
6. Translate segments into evidence-based, testable marketing hypotheses.

# Dataset Description

```{r dataset}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Item = c("Dataset type", "Source file", "Rows", "Columns", "Note"),
                        Value = c(info$Dataset_Type[1], info$Source_File[1], info$Rows[1], info$Columns[1], info$Note[1])),
             caption = "Dataset used in this run")
```

Variables used: **CustomerID** (identifier, never used for clustering), **Gender** (categorical, used only for description), **Age** (years), **Annual_Income** (thousand dollars) and **Spending_Score** (index from 1 to 100 assigned by the retailer). Full details, license and limitations are in `data/README.md`.

# Data Cleaning

```{r cleaning}
knitr::kable(quality, col.names = c("Check", "Value"), caption = "Data quality summary")
```

The cleaning strategy never modifies the raw file and never silently deletes valid observations:

- exact duplicate rows are removed and logged; conflicting identifiers stop the pipeline for manual review;
- missing numeric values are median-imputed only when they affect at most 5% of rows;
- out-of-range values and IQR outliers are **flagged and kept**, because extreme but plausible customers (for example very high earners) are exactly what a segmentation should capture.

```{r outliers}
knitr::kable(outl, caption = "Outlier summary using the 1.5 x IQR rule (observations retained)")
```

# Methodology

1. **Feature selection:** Age, Annual_Income and Spending_Score. CustomerID and Gender are excluded from the model.
2. **Standardisation:** each feature is converted to a z-score with `scale()` so that variables measured on different scales contribute equally to Euclidean distances.
3. **K-means clustering:** `stats::kmeans()` with `nstart = 50` random restarts and a fixed seed for reproducibility.
4. **Evaluation:** within-cluster sum of squares (elbow method) and average silhouette width (`cluster::silhouette()`).
5. **Visualisation:** principal component analysis (PCA) projects the three standardised features onto two dimensions.
6. **Interpretation:** clusters are profiled in original units and labelled from their observed statistics.

No labels or outcome variables are used, so there is no train/test split and no target leakage; scaling and clustering use exactly the same feature columns.

# Optimal Cluster Selection

```{r eval-table}
knitr::kable(eval_k, caption = "Cluster evaluation for each candidate K")
```

```{r eval-plots, fig.cap="Elbow method and silhouette analysis."}
knitr::include_graphics(c(plot_path("elbow_plot.png"), plot_path("silhouette_analysis.png")))
```

Choosing K needs interpretation; **no single metric decides it**. The elbow is often ambiguous and the silhouette can keep rising for larger K even when extra clusters add little business value. This project reports both metrics and applies a transparent starting rule: choose the smallest K of at least 3 whose silhouette is within 0.03 of the best silhouette. This run selected **K = `r k_final`**. The choice should always be checked against the segment profiles below, and can be overridden with `CONFIG$k_final` in `R/01_data_loading.R`.

# Customer Segment Profiles

```{r profile-table}
knitr::kable(prof[, c("Cluster", "Segment", "Customers", "Percent", "Avg_Age", "Avg_Annual_Income", "Avg_Spending_Score")],
             caption = "Segment profiles (Avg_Annual_Income in thousand dollars; Avg_Spending_Score on a 1-100 scale)")
```

Labels are assigned from the data: a segment's average income and spending score are compared with the overall averages (z-scores with a +/-0.5 threshold). The evidence for each label:

```{r label-evidence, results='asis'}
cat(paste0("- **", prof$Segment, "**: ", prof$Rationale, ".", collapse = "\n"), "\n")
```

# Business Insights

> **Read this first:** these are **hypotheses to test** (for example with A/B tests), not proven causal effects. Segments describe observed behaviour. No churn data exists in this dataset and no churn model is implemented.

```{r recs, results='asis'}
for (i in seq_len(nrow(recs))) {
  r <- recs[i, ]
  cat("### ", r$Segment, "\n\n", sep = "")
  cat("- **Evidence:** ", r$Evidence, "\n", sep = "")
  cat("- **Recommended action:** ", r$Recommended_Action, "\n", sep = "")
  cat("- **Hypothesis to test:** ", r$Hypothesis_To_Test, "\n", sep = "")
  cat("- **Suggested KPIs:** ", r$Suggested_KPIs, "\n\n", sep = "")
}
```

# Limitations

- `r if (is_synthetic) "This run uses a synthetic dataset, so the segments illustrate the method rather than real customer behaviour." else "The Mall Customers dataset is a small (200-row) teaching dataset whose collection method is not documented."`
- Only three variables are used; real segmentation would add purchase history, recency, frequency, product categories and channel.
- Spending Score is an index defined by the data provider, not revenue or profit.
- K-means assumes roughly spherical clusters of similar size and is sensitive to outliers and scaling choices.
- The number of clusters is a judgement call; different reasonable K values give different segmentations.
- Segments are a snapshot in time; customer behaviour changes.
- Recommendations are untested hypotheses, and no churn prediction is performed.

# Future Enhancements

- Add recency-frequency-monetary (RFM) features from transaction data.
- Compare k-means with hierarchical clustering, k-medoids (PAM) and Gaussian mixture models, and check segment stability with bootstrapping.
- Build a Shiny dashboard for interactive exploration.
- Run controlled A/B tests of the recommended actions to measure real campaign uplift.
- With genuine churn data, add a supervised churn model using the segments as features.

# Conclusion

The pipeline produced **`r k_final` customer segments** from `r n_customers` customers: `r paste(prof$Segment, collapse = "; ")`. The segments are reproducible (fixed seed), based on standardised features, evaluated with two complementary metrics, and translated into testable marketing hypotheses. They give marketing teams a data-driven starting point for targeting, to be validated with experiments and richer data.
